---
title: "Revision and integration"
---

These are formative study tasks, not an official examination or a prediction
of its questions. Attempt each explanation before opening the feedback. Include
the causal chain: structure or signal → process → physiological consequence.

## Animal half {#animal-half}

### 1. From tissue to oxygen demand

Compare a thin exchange epithelium with a thick stratified protective epithelium.
Explain why their structures suit different functions. Then trace how an increase
in muscle oxygen demand can be met through ventilation, exchange and circulation.
Name one observation you would need before classifying a real tissue section.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

A short diffusion distance favours exchange; multiple layers can protect
against abrasion. Neither alone identifies an organ. Cell shape, layering,
lumen, extracellular material and neighbouring tissues provide evidence.
Ventilation renews the respiratory medium, diffusion crosses the exchange
barrier, blood flow distributes oxygen, and tissues extract it. Increased
demand need not be met by changing just one step. Microscopy interpretation
must use the actual image and scale, not a guessed label from a written clue.
:::

### 2. Energy and temperature

Two simulated animals consume 18 and 30 µmol oxygen over six minutes. Both
have mass 0.5 g. Calculate the whole-animal and mass-specific mean rates.
The animals differ in both temperature and feeding history. What comparison
is possible, and what causal claim is unsupported?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

Whole-animal rates are 3 and 5 µmol min⁻¹. Mass-specific values are 6 and
10 µmol min⁻¹ g⁻¹. The observed rates differ, but temperature and feeding
history are confounded; neither cause can be isolated. Oxygen consumption
is an indicator of aerobic metabolism under the stated conditions, not a
direct measure of all energy use or a fitness score.
:::

### 3. Two osmotic environments

Compare the water-balance problems faced by a freshwater fish and a terrestrial
mammal. Explain how exchange surfaces, ion transport and excretion contribute.
Why does “water follows salt” fail as a complete explanation of kidney function?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

A typical freshwater teleost gains water osmotically and loses ions across
permeable surfaces; dilute urine and active ion uptake help maintain balance.
A terrestrial mammal loses water to the environment and must balance intake,
metabolic production and losses. Kidney filtration, selective reabsorption,
secretion, medullary gradients and regulated collecting-duct permeability
all matter. Water movement depends on a pathway as well as a driving gradient.
There are diverse exceptions to broad group descriptions.
:::

### 4. A signal to movement

Explain how a neural signal can produce skeletal-muscle force, and how endocrine
signals can influence the resources available for activity. Distinguish changes
in action-potential frequency from changes in action-potential amplitude.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

In a vertebrate example, a motor neuron activates the neuromuscular junction,
muscle membrane excitation triggers calcium release, and calcium permits
actin–myosin interaction. ATP supports cross-bridge cycling and calcium handling.
Recruitment and activation frequency contribute to force regulation. Hormones
can alter fuel mobilisation and longer-term tissue properties. A stronger
stimulus generally changes firing/recruitment rather than scaling each
regenerative action potential as if it were an analogue voltage signal.
:::

## Plant half {#plant-half}

### 5. Water and carbon together

Explain how dry air can increase the demand for water loss, why stomatal closure
can reduce that loss, and how closure can constrain carbon assimilation. Does
this imply every leaf under drought has the same photosynthetic rate?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

Water-vapour loss depends on the vapour gradient and pathway conductance.
Closing stomata lowers conductance but also restricts CO₂ entry. Leaf temperature,
boundary layer, soil/root hydraulic supply, biochemistry, species and acclimation
also matter. Describe a trade-off and its conditions, not a universal numerical
response. Stomata are regulated pores, rather than actively pumping water vapour.
:::

### 6. Net exchange is a balance

A teaching model gives gross fixation of 14 and respiratory loss of 3
µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ under one light condition. Calculate net uptake. In a second
condition net uptake is zero. Does zero net uptake show that all metabolism
has stopped? What extra assumption would be needed to estimate gross fixation
from a dark-respiration measurement?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

Net uptake is 11 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ under the supplied simplified balance.
Zero net uptake means opposing fluxes balance; processes can remain active.
Using a dark rate to correct a light measurement assumes the relevant
respiratory loss is suitably represented under illumination. Real measurements
can also involve photorespiration and condition-dependent fluxes. State what
the teaching model includes before interpreting it as a full carbon budget.
:::

### 7. A developmental response

Propose how to distinguish failure of seed germination from failure to supply
permissive conditions. Include viability, water, temperature, light where
relevant, and dormancy. Explain why a hormone response depends on tissue and stage.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

Use a suitable viable seed lot, record environmental conditions, include an
appropriate reference and define germination before counting. Non-germination
can reflect dead seeds, unsuitable conditions or dormancy; the observation
alone does not distinguish them. Hormone responses depend on receptors,
downstream machinery, sensitivity, other signals and developmental competence.
Different tissues need not respond identically to the same external dose.
:::

### 8. An application claim

A line of modified plants has greater dry mass than its comparison line in
one controlled trial. Draft a conclusion about the observation, then list
evidence needed before recommending deployment under field drought.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

The observed dry-mass difference applies to the measured lines and conditions.
Check independent allocation, genetic-background controls, replication,
measurement timing and water use. Field performance, yield, environmental
interactions, non-target effects, management, access and stakeholder priorities
need evidence. Neither the modification method alone nor greater biomass in
one setting determines the whole benefit–risk judgement.
:::

## Integrating both halves

### 9. Transport is gradient plus pathway

Make a comparison table for a gill, a kidney epithelial pathway and a root-to-leaf
water pathway. For each identify the transported substance, driving force,
barrier/pathway, regulatory process and a cost or limitation. Do not assume
that all three use the same mechanism because all transport material.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback

Gill oxygen crosses along a partial-pressure gradient; ventilation and blood
flow help maintain it. Kidney epithelia combine selective channels/transporters
with ion gradients and regulated water permeability. Root-to-leaf water flow
depends on water-potential differences and hydraulic pathways, with evaporation
and stomatal regulation important in transpiring plants. Diffusion distance,
energy for gradient maintenance and hydraulic resistance impose different
constraints. Distinguish bulk flow from membrane transport.
:::

### 10. Evidence before an explanation

Choose one supplied practical dataset. Write five sentences: the question;
the independent unit and comparison; a result with units; a mechanism consistent
with that result; and a limitation or alternative explanation. Draw the result
without using R. Swap explanations with a partner and identify any sentence
that states more than the design supports.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Feedback criteria

A complete response separates observation from mechanism and mechanism from
proof. The calculation and figure must match the data dictionary. An explanation
should be consistent with the unit tutorial, while the limitation should name
a specific design/measurement issue. No particular software or p-value is
required to achieve this.
:::
